slice: Resolve original grouping keys in HAVING and ORDER BY
status: optional two-file Rust resolver patch; default vendor unchanged

protocol.json.hypothesis: Explicit GROUPING/GROUPING_ID in ORDER BY should match the original key despite the float grouping normalizer alias. Inspect all shared metadata helper callers.

supplement-protocol.json.why: Separate hidden ORDER BY attributes from HAVING key resolution; cover rollup/cube/sets/duplicates, explicit functions, raw keys, computed and qualified keys, multiple keys and invalid arguments. Keep the initial 12 queries unchanged.

bindings-protocol.json.scope: Exercise HAVING field bindings across mixed grouping sets, aliases and field-preserving filters/windows; retain ambiguous projection alias rejection.

case-protocol.json.why: Name lookup uses ASCII-insensitive comparison; test repeated grouping bindings with differently cased column/alias references. Check original Spark behavior and an outer-filter equivalent separately.

alias-sort-protocol.json.why: An explicit GROUPING_ID sort must retain the bitmap width for distinct alias fields, even if their normalized input expression is identical.

alias-identity-protocol.json.why: Distinct aliases of the same input expression must retain the grouping bitmap width and field identities. Argument matching may ignore aliases without collapsing physical keys.

implementation.rule: Reuse named grouping-expression expansion for HAVING bindings and aggregate outputs. Deduplicate HAVING names with the same ASCII-insensitive comparison as lookup. Compare grouping-function arguments without aliases while preserving physical grouping-key identities. Remove only the internal floating normalizer from sort metadata. Follow field-preserving Filter/Window nodes to find the aggregate.
implementation.reuse: Existing native grouping and expression execution. No new runtime kernel, node, dependency or Python execution path. Build the HAVING scope only when a HAVING clause exists.

alias_sort_parent_check.scope: Preserve native parent values and row order for its two-key layout. Spark canonicalizes the aliases to one key; that separate incompatibility remains.

first_candidate.reason_for_revision: Normalize HAVING name bindings with the lookup case rule, compare grouping arguments without aliases, and deduplicate physical keys before peeling internal normalizers.

iterations.regression_audit: initial-audit-failure.log catches the legacy duplicate-HAVING query changing from matching errors to success. A separately recorded outer-filter Spark reference validates the successful result; its original strict difference remains visible.
iterations.protocols: Initial, supplemental and binding SQL were frozen before implementation. Case/alias follow-ups and semantic references record their later introduction explicitly.

alias_canonicalization_boundary.scope: A pre-existing structural grouping-key canonicalization difference, separate from resolving valid key references in HAVING/ORDER BY.
alias_canonicalization_boundary.observed: Spark treats k1 and k2 aliases of the same input expression as one semantic grouping key, retaining duplicate grouping-set rows. The current native plan retains two fields and yields IDs 0,1,3 rather than 0,0,1.
alias_canonicalization_boundary.acceptance_for_current_slice: Retain this Spark difference. The explicit GROUPING_ID sort must preserve the existing native bitmap width and row order; compare it with the unchanged parent output to catch the first candidate regression. Do not present the parent output as Spark-compatible.
alias_canonicalization_boundary.next_slice: Canonicalize aliases in grouping expressions and expand ROLLUP/CUBE with repeated semantic keys into explicit grouping sets while preserving duplicate rows, field names and bit positions. Reuse the existing DataFusion grouping-set execution path.

performance_protocol.purpose: Measure shared grouping metadata and HAVING-scope changes on already-correct integer ROLLUP and ordinary grouping/projection controls.
performance_protocol.inference: Use process medians, paired quartet log ratios and fixed seed 172 / 10000 bootstrap resamples. Retain all controls and observations.
performance_protocol.runtime: c7b4e92 optional runtime with grouping-function resolution fix
performance_protocol.input_limit: 512 integer keys and a nonduplicate grand total produce 513 sorted IDs. Duplicate and full-width correctness is covered separately in the SQL corpus.

performance_findings: All 160 fresh processes and all 41 samples retained, with full counter coverage, no migrations and unchanged governor/ASLR. No builds or other investigations ran during measurement.

All paired planning latency intervals span zero. GROUPING_ID planning changes by -0.183 percent, interval [-0.525,0.254], with -0.059 percent instructions; ordinary grouping changes by -0.293 percent, interval [-1.523,0.805], with -0.061 percent instructions.

GROUPING_ID and ordinary grouping execution latency intervals span zero. Execution instruction changes are at most 0.001 percent. The unchanged projection control rises 0.554 percent, interval [0.114,1.102], with unchanged instruction work; retain this observation without claiming causal overhead or universal equivalence.
Same-binary controls include +0.848 percent ordinary-grouping planning and +0.415 percent execution. All controls remain in the archive.

The preceding public GROUPING_ID planning cost of about 9 percent, and earlier floating normalization/widening costs, remain open. These measurements use already-correct parent queries, not newly enabled syntax.
limitations: 12 new alias observations still differ. Spark canonicalizes two aliases of one expression into one grouping key; native planning currently keeps two. The first candidate introduced an additional ordering error in that native layout; the final candidate restores the parent ordering.

50 new original Spark error observations execute with results matching equivalent queries; two earlier duplicate-HAVING observations do the same. Keep these as explicit original Spark differences under the accepted SQL semantic policy.
The 6068 older observations remain 5753 agreements. Their comparator checks values, types and error stages, not complete error identity or metadata.
34 Rust planner tests cover resolution and execution. 116 real-Delta captures compare complete schemas and rows; this does not establish complete Spark or Delta compatibility.
The performance comparison covers already-correct integer ROLLUP, ordinary integer grouping and projection. Newly enabled query forms have no successful unmodified-parent timing baseline.
Earlier float normalization/widening costs and the public GROUPING_ID masking cost remain separate; no universal zero-overhead claim.
